lead: This unit is about defending systems after cryptography is in place: firewalls, intrusion detection, honeypots, program and operating system security, access control, risk management, cloud services and AI-based detection. After it you can choose a firewall configuration, read UNIX and Windows permissions, explain a buffer overflow, compare access control models, compute a simple risk figure, and describe how cloud and machine-learning security services are used and attacked.
about: The unit moves from network edges to code, operating systems, policy and cloud. Chapter 6.1 explains firewalls and where to place them; 6.2 adds intrusion detection and prevention; 6.3 uses honeypots as decoys. Chapter 6.4 looks inside programs at buffer overflows and malicious code, and 6.5 applies the same thinking to UNIX and Windows protection, authorization and vulnerabilities. Chapter 6.6 compares access control models, 6.7 turns controls into policy, risk treatment and audit. Chapter 6.8 covers cloud security services and shared responsibility, and 6.9 adds AI anomaly detection and adversarial attacks. Each chapter assumes the earlier one and points back to Units 1–5 for attacks, cryptography and protocols.

chapters.idea: A firewall is a policy enforcement point that allows or denies traffic between networks according to ordered rules.
chapters.depth: Cover packet-filtering, stateful inspection, application-level proxy and next-generation firewall ideas. Configurations: screening router, dual-homed host, screened host, screened subnet or DMZ. Explain ordered rule tables, default deny, ingress and egress filtering, logging, and NAT as a configuration aid. Some syllabi call packet filtering a screening router. Only a few universities teach next-generation firewall and UTM details; keep short. VPN and TLS belong to Unit 5.

figure.title: Screened subnet
figure.aria: Internet traffic passes through a border router to a firewall, which sends allowed web and mail traffic to a DMZ and allowed VPN traffic to the internal LAN.

chapters.example: A stateless firewall has rules in order: 1 allow TCP from 10.0.0.0/24 to 192.168.1.10 port 443; 2 deny TCP any to 192.168.1.10 port 23; 3 allow TCP any to 192.168.1.10 port 80; 4 deny all. State the decision for packets: (a) 10.0.0.5:50000 to 192.168.1.10:443, (b) 8.8.8.8:40000 to 192.168.1.10:23, (c) 10.0.0.5:50001 to 192.168.1.10:22. Answers: (a) allow by rule 1; (b) deny by rule 2; (c) no allow matches, so rule 4 denies.
chapters.trap: Default allow is a common mistake; the first matching rule wins, so order matters. A stateful firewall keeps a connection table and does not need a separate reverse rule for replies.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 network attacks and port scanning; Unit 5 VPN basics.
chapters.leave: IDS and IPS detail to 6.2, honeypots to 6.3, TLS and IPsec to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: An IDS detects suspicious activity and raises alerts; an IPS sits inline and can also block it.
chapters.depth: Host-based and network-based IDS; signature, anomaly and stateful protocol detection; passive IDS versus inline IPS; sensor placement, promiscuous mode, alerts, tuning, false positives and false negatives; simple rule format. Some syllabi call this network intrusion detection and prevention systems. Add a short note that an IDS can watch routing announcements for BGP hijack anomalies; full BGP security is outside this unit. Only a few universities teach advanced BGP security; keep short.

figure.title: IDS versus IPS
figure.aria: Traffic reaches a sensor and detection engine; in IDS mode the engine sends an alert, and in IPS mode it can send a packet to an inline blocker that drops it.

chapters.example: Over one hour a signature IDS sees 1000 packets: 20 are real attacks and 980 are normal. It raises 48 alerts: 18 attacks and 30 normal packets. Compute detection rate, false positive rate and precision. Detection rate = 18/20 = 0.90 or 90%. False positive rate = 30/980 = 0.0306 or 3.06%. Precision = 18/48 = 0.375 or 37.5%.
chapters.trap: An IDS cannot stop traffic by itself; an IPS can block but may also drop legitimate traffic. Anomaly detectors often produce many false positives when normal traffic is huge.
chapters.prereq: 6.1 firewall placement; Unit 1 attacks and malware.
chapters.leave: Honeypot design to 6.3; audit policy to 6.7; full protocol security to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: A honeypot is a decoy system whose only purpose is to attract and record attacks.
chapters.depth: Low-interaction versus high-interaction honeypots; production versus research use; honeynets, decoy services, containment, logging, data control, legal and ethical issues. Show how a firewall redirects unused addresses and an IDS watches the honeynet. Some syllabi call these deception systems. Keep setup simple; no exploit writing. Only a few universities teach high-interaction honeynets in detail; keep short.

figure.title: Honeynet behind a firewall
figure.aria: A firewall redirects unused addresses to a honeynet switch that connects low-interaction and high-interaction decoys, while an IDS sensor watches a mirror port.

chapters.example: A honeynet uses 10.0.0.0/28. The network address is 10.0.0.0 and the broadcast address is 10.0.0.15. Reserve 10.0.0.1 for the gateway and 10.0.0.2 for the IDS sensor. How many usable addresses remain for honeypots? A /28 has 16 addresses, 14 usable hosts. After reserving 2, 12 addresses remain for honeypots.
chapters.trap: A honeypot is not a production service; any traffic to it is suspicious, but an attacker who escapes a virtual machine can reach the local network. Keep it contained and never inside the trusted zone.
chapters.prereq: 6.1 firewall rules; 6.2 IDS monitoring; Unit 1 attacks.
chapters.leave: Malware analysis detail to 6.4; cloud honeypots to 6.8.

chapters.idea: Many program attacks exploit memory-safety bugs, and malicious code is a separate class of program threat.
chapters.depth: Cover memory layout: text, data, heap, stack; unsafe C functions such as gets, strcpy, sprintf; stack buffer overflow, off-by-one, integer overflow, heap overflow basics, format strings. Explain code reuse and ROP at a high level, memory mapping, and malicious code classes: virus, worm, trojan, logic bomb, backdoor. Controls: safe libraries, stack canaries, NX/DEP, ASLR, control-flow integrity, static and dynamic analysis. Only a few universities teach ROP and CFI in detail; keep short. Penetration testing is in 6.7.

figure.title: 32-bit stack frame
figure.aria: A stack frame has eight buffer bytes followed by the saved frame pointer EBP and the return address EIP.

chapters.example: A 32-bit function has char buf[8]; it calls strcpy(buf, input). Saved EBP is 4 bytes and the return address is 4 bytes. Input is 16 bytes: bytes 1–8 are 'A', bytes 9–12 are 'B', bytes 13–16 are a0 84 04 08. (a) Which stack fields are overwritten? (b) What return address is used in little-endian? (c) Why is the null terminator a problem? Answers: (a) buffer, saved EBP and return address; (b) 0x080484a0; (c) strcpy also writes a null byte after byte 16, corrupting the next word.
chapters.trap: The null terminator from strcpy adds one byte, so an off-by-one can overwrite the saved frame pointer. ASLR is probabilistic and does not fix the underlying bug.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 malware basics; C memory layout.
chapters.leave: OS-level permissions to 6.5; audit and penetration testing to 6.7; adversarial ML to 6.9.

chapters.idea: Operating system security depends on protection mechanisms, authorization checks and disciplined vulnerability management.
chapters.depth: UNIX: users and groups, rwx mode bits, chmod, chown, umask, setuid, setgid, sticky bit, /etc/passwd and shadow, superuser, SUID and PATH vulnerabilities, security analysis. Windows: SIDs, access tokens, security descriptors, DACL and SACL, ACEs, integrity levels, UAC, services, registry, patch management. Cover hardening, least privilege, auditing and vulnerability analysis. Explain security kernels and reference monitors, and retrofitting security into a commercial OS. Only a few universities teach security kernels and retrofitting in depth; keep short. ASLR and CFI are in 6.4.

figure.title: Operating system access check
figure.aria: A process token and an object ACL are compared in an access check, which produces allow or deny and records the result in an audit log.

chapters.example: A file is owned by root, group auditors, mode 4755. User alice is not root and not in auditors. She runs the program. (a) What do the four octal digits mean? (b) Can she execute it? (c) What is her effective UID inside the program? (d) Why may setuid be ignored? Answers: (a) 4 is setuid; owner rwx; group r-x; other r-x. (b) Yes, other has execute. (c) Effective UID is root because the setuid owner is root. (d) Setuid is ignored on filesystems mounted nosuid, on scripts, or when execute permission is missing.
chapters.trap: setuid changes the effective UID, not the real UID. In Windows, a deny ACE usually wins over allow. Root can override UNIX permission bits but not every security control.
chapters.leave: Access control models to 6.6; cloud IAM to 6.8; CPU scheduling and semaphores to an OS lab.

chapters.idea: Access control decides which subject may perform which operation on which object, using a model and an enforcement policy.
chapters.depth: Access matrix, ACLs and capabilities; DAC, MAC with Bell-LaPadula (no read up, no write down), Biba briefly; RBAC with roles and separation of duties; ABAC with attributes. Policy enforcement, least privilege, privilege creep. Only a few universities teach biometric access control; give FAR and FRR in one short paragraph. Keep formal security models light.

figure.title: Access matrix
figure.aria: An access matrix lists Alice, Bob and Carol against files f1, f2 and f3, with rights such as r, w and x in each cell.

chapters.example: Access matrix rows Alice, Bob, Carol; columns f1, f2, f3. Alice: rw on f1, r on f2. Bob: r on f1, rw on f2, x on f3. Carol: r on f2, rwx on f3. (a) Can Bob write f2? (b) Can Carol read f1? (c) Give an ACL for f2. (d) Give a capability list for Bob. Answers: (a) yes; (b) no; (c) Alice r, Bob rw, Carol r; (d) f1 r, f2 rw, f3 x.
chapters.trap: An ACL is stored per object, while a capability is held per subject. MAC uses labels, not user identity. RBAC is not the same as a UNIX group.
chapters.leave: Organizational policy and risk to 6.7; cloud IAM to 6.8.

chapters.idea: Security policy turns business rules into controls, and risk management decides which controls are worth paying for.
chapters.depth: Policy hierarchy: policy, standard, procedure, guideline. Risk elements: asset, threat, vulnerability, likelihood, impact; risk treatment avoid, reduce, transfer, accept; risk register and security program drivers. Information security risk management activities and framework. Laws and regulations: FISMA 2002, GLBA, HIPAA; ISO 27001 and ISO 27005. Audit, logging, monitoring, compliance evidence, vulnerability assessment and penetration testing. Keep legal detail factual. Only a few universities teach blockchain audit logs; one line at most.

figure.title: 5 by 5 risk matrix
figure.aria: A five-by-five risk matrix multiplies likelihood from 1 to 5 by impact from 1 to 5, giving risk scores from 1 to 25.

chapters.example: An asset is worth ₹10,00,000. A threat exploits a vulnerability with exposure factor 25% and annualized rate of occurrence 0.2. (a) Compute single loss expectancy. (b) Compute annualized loss expectancy. (c) A control costs ₹60,000 per year and reduces ALE to ₹20,000. Is it cost-effective? SLE = 10,00,000 × 0.25 = ₹2,50,000. ALE = 2,50,000 × 0.2 = ₹50,000. Saving = ₹30,000, cost = ₹60,000, so it is not cost-effective by this simple measure.
chapters.trap: Risk is not the same as threat or vulnerability. Compliance with a law does not by itself make a system secure. ALE uses the annual rate of occurrence.
chapters.prereq: 6.6 access control policy; Unit 1 threats and vulnerabilities.
chapters.leave: Cloud shared responsibility to 6.8; AI detection to 6.9.

chapters.idea: In cloud computing the provider secures the platform and the customer secures its own configuration, data and identities.
chapters.depth: IaaS, PaaS and SaaS; shared responsibility; IAM, security groups, encryption at rest and in transit, key management, WAF, logging and monitoring, backup, isolation and multi-tenancy, compliance and incident response. Provider services versus customer duties. Only a few universities teach hardware-rooted cloud security: TEE, HSM, side-channel and bit-flipping risks, and embedded device security; keep short. Some syllabi add blockchain-as-a-service and cryptocurrency custody as service examples; one line only.

figure.title: Cloud responsibility stack
figure.aria: A cloud stack from data and application down to operating system, hypervisor and hardware, with customer responsibility greater at the top and provider responsibility greater at the bottom.

chapters.example: A SaaS CRM has 500 users in 3 roles. The provider offers encryption at rest with customer-managed keys, MFA, and 90-day audit logs. The customer assigns roles. For each control say whether it is mainly provider or customer responsibility: (a) physical security of the data centre, (b) key policy that decides who can decrypt, (c) role assignment for the 500 users, (d) hypervisor patching. Answers: (a) provider; (b) customer for key policy with customer-managed keys; (c) customer; (d) provider.
chapters.trap: Moving to cloud does not transfer all responsibility. Encryption at rest does not protect data in use. A public storage bucket is usually a customer configuration error, not a provider break-in.
chapters.prereq: 6.6 access control; 6.7 risk assessment; Unit 5 TLS basics.
chapters.leave: TLS and VPN details to Unit 5; AI anomaly detection to 6.9; full virtualization course material elsewhere.

chapters.idea: AI can learn normal behaviour and flag anomalies, but attackers can also manipulate the model and its inputs.
chapters.depth: Anomaly detection: supervised and unsupervised, features, training and validation, thresholds, false positives. Use in intrusion detection, malware analysis and threat intelligence. Adversarial machine learning: evasion, poisoning, perturbation, model extraction; defences: adversarial training, robust features, human review. Keep neural network math light. Only a few universities teach deep learning and NLP for threat intelligence; keep short.

figure.title: Anomaly threshold
figure.aria: A threshold line at score 0.70; normal scores stay below it and three of four attack scores are above it.

chapters.example: An anomaly detector gives scores from 0 to 1 with threshold 0.70. Normal scores: 0.10, 0.20, 0.35, 0.55. Attack scores: 0.65, 0.80, 0.90, 0.95. (a) Which are flagged? (b) Compute TPR and FPR at 0.70. (c) If the 0.80 attack is perturbed to 0.60, what is the new TPR? Answers: (a) 0.80, 0.90, 0.95 are flagged; (b) TPR = 3/4 = 0.75, FPR = 0/4 = 0; (c) flagged attacks become 0.90 and 0.95, so TPR = 2/4 = 0.50.
chapters.trap: High accuracy on imbalanced data is misleading because most samples are normal. Anomaly detection is not signature detection, and adversarial perturbations can be hard to see.
chapters.leave: Deep learning training details to ML courses; cryptographic and protocol details to Units 3–5.
